applicationDates: EJATT runs continuous weekly walk-in registration (every Wednesday, 9–11am, Alsip) rather than a single once-a-year opening day. The aptitude exam itself is given twice a year, in September and March — you're told your specific test date only after you register. As posted on EJATT's own FAQ, the cycle open now runs registration through February 2027, feeding the March 2027 test. Separately, watch ejatt.com for the Trainee Program's own registration window, which opens for a few weeks and accepts only the first 500 registrants.
exam:
EJATT's own aptitude test — the exact vendor/section format isn't published on ejatt.com. EJATT hands its own official study guide directly to every applicant when they return their completed PEF — that guide is the reliable source for what's actually on it.
Algebra & math
Reading comprehension
EJATT doesn't publish a minimum score; no sponsor is required. Selection runs on a points system, not just the aptitude test — points also come from completing the Jumpstart program, prior construction experience, veteran status, a college degree, and (the single biggest boost) acceptance into the Trainee Program.
Not published by EJATT; the practical wait is until the next posted registration/testing cycle.
preparation:
Take any building/construction coursework at your high school or community college. Examples of courses are construction safety, shop, drafting, or basic arc welding. These count as real experience on an application, even without a job in the trade yet.
Nail down the algebra requirement first — it's a hard document check, not just test prep. If a student doesn't have a qualifying HS Algebra grade, EJATT itself points applicants to a free Online Tech Math class at skillsprep.org whose completion certificate satisfies the requirement.
Whichever version of the test Local 134 uses, math is central — refresh fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios, and solving basic algebraic equations (solve for X); no calculator is permitted on these tests generally.
No prior electrical knowledge is tested on any version — it's aptitude, not trade knowledge.
Use EJATT's own study guide (handed out when you return your PEF) as the primary prep material; treat third-party guides as backup, not gospel, given the disagreement over exact format.
Score isn't the only lever: selection runs on a points system, so completing Jumpstart, documenting construction experience or veteran status, and especially getting into the Trainee Program all add points on top of the aptitude test itself — treat those as seriously as studying for the exam.
The Trainee Program's own registration window is short (posted on ejatt.com a few weeks out) and capped at the first 500 people — if a student wants this route, they need to watch ejatt.com closely and be ready to register the moment it opens, since applicants have lined up hours in advance.

steps.title: Complete HS Algebra I with a C or better
steps.explanation: EJATT looks for one full year of HS-level Algebra I (or a higher-level course), grade of C or better, as part of your file — a GED Math Certification does not satisfy this. If you've already taken the course but don't feel up to date on your skills, that's exactly what the Jumpstart program below is for.

steps.title: Register in person, any Wednesday

EJATT (the Electrical Joint Apprenticeship & Training Trust — Local 134's training arm, run as “IN-Tech”) takes walk-in registration for both the Electrical Construction and Communications programs.

Go Here to Apply

Your valid driver's license

steps.title: Come back with your Personal Experience Form

You'll leave visit one with a Personal Experience Form (PEF) to complete off-site

And proof of one year of HS-level Algebra (grade of C or better); a GED Math Certification does not count

Return the completed PEF, and the documents, by the posted deadline on a later visit

steps.title: Receive your test date
steps.explanation: When you return your completed PEF, EJATT hands you its own official aptitude-test study guide plus a letter with your specific test date and time — tests run twice a year, in September and March.

steps.title: Sign up for Jumpstart
steps.explanation: At registration you'll also be told about EJATT's Jumpstart program: a single Saturday, 8 hours, reviewing the skills needed for the aptitude exam. Jumpstart is worth doing for two separate reasons — it's real exam prep, and completing it adds points to your file.

steps.title: Get hands-on experience
steps.explanation: EJATT selection is a points-based system, not a simple pass/fail cutoff on the aptitude exam. Along with your test score, points also come from completing Jumpstart, prior construction experience, veteran status, and a college degree — so a strong aptitude score alone doesn't guarantee a spot, and it's worth documenting anything in your background that could add points. any college math, CAD, or drafting class is specifically recommended, and college credit of any sort generally helps strengthen a file, even outside those specific subjects.

steps.title: Register for the Trainee Program
steps.explanation: EJATT's own pre-apprenticeship program, the Trainee Program, is described by Local 134 as by far the largest point boost available — and it's paid, at 35% of the journeyman rate, while you're in it. It's posted on ejatt.com a few weeks before its own separate registration window opens, and only the first 500 people to register are accepted — due to demand, applicants have been known to line up hours before registration opens. Getting into the Trainee Program adds a large number of points toward your apprenticeship file, on top of whatever your test score and other points add up to.

steps.title: Take Aptitude Test
steps.explanation: Test date lands on the cycle's posted testing month — September or March (see “Current application dates” below). You'll be notified by email within about 8 weeks of testing whether you're selected. The number of apprentices selected depends on the needs of the industry and may vary from cycle to cycle — a strong test score doesn't guarantee a spot in every cycle, especially once points from Jumpstart, the Trainee Program, and other factors are all factored in for every applicant.

An electrician needs ¾ of a 250-foot spool of wire for a job. How many feet of wire is that?
What number comes next in the series: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ___
questions.explanation: The gap between terms increases by 2 each time (3, 5, 7, 9…), so the next gap is 11: 26 + 11 = 37.

Applicants leave their first visit with a form to complete at home, since same-day submissions are not accepted; they return the completed form on a later visit, along with proof of high school graduation and one year of qualifying Algebra coursework.” Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: Applicants can register and submit all paperwork in a single visit.
The registration process requires at least two separate visits.
Algebra coursework is optional for applicants.
Registration happens only once per year.
questions.explanation: The passage says applicants leave with a form to complete “at home” and “return on a later visit” — that's two visits at minimum, matching how EJATT's own registration actually works.

questions.prompt: Two identical 4-ohm resistors are connected in series to a 12-volt battery. Using I = V ÷ R, what is the total current in the circuit?
questions.explanation: In series, resistances add: 4 + 4 = 8 ohms. I = 12V ÷ 8Ω = 1.5 amps.

questions.prompt: Solve for x: 3x + 7 = 2x + 15
A job needs 3 conduit runs of 8.5 feet each and 2 runs of 6.25 feet each. What's the total length of conduit needed?
What number comes next in the series: 3, 6, 12, 24, ___
questions.explanation: Each term doubles the one before it: 24 × 2 = 48.

Points are also awarded for completing the Jumpstart program, prior construction experience, veteran status, and a college degree. Selection is based on several factors, not the test score alone.
Veterans receive no consideration in the process.
A college degree disqualifies an applicant.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly names several other factors besides the test score, and says the score alone “does not guarantee a spot” — selection is clearly multi-factor.

questions.explanation: Meshed gears always rotate in opposite directions from one another.

reference.description: An electrician installs, maintains, and troubleshoots the wiring, power distribution, and control systems inside buildings — pulling conduit, running cable, reading blueprints, and wiring panels. Chicago-area IBEW/NECA electricians work across data centers, hospitals, high-rises, and everything in between, in both new construction and renovation.
reference.blurb: Installs and maintains the wiring and power systems inside buildings.

tracks.name: Electrical Construction (“A”)
tracks.short: Wires and maintains electrical systems in new construction and existing buildings.
tracks.covers: Assembles, installs, maintains, and tests electrical equipment and supporting components — power distribution, power generation, energy storage, and renewable energy production. This is the traditional “inside wireman” path: conduit, panels, blueprints, commercial and industrial buildings.

tracks.name: Communications (“C”)
tracks.short: Installs and maintains low-voltage data, security, and network cabling.
tracks.covers: Installs and maintains structured cabling and electronic systems — card access, nurse call, CCTV, security, and networking — across residential, commercial, and industrial sites. Lower-voltage, more IT/network-adjacent work than the Construction track.

reference.tracksIntro: EJATT/IN-Tech doesn't run a single “electrician” apprenticeship. It runs two separate programs, and a student has to pick a lane (though you can register for both — see below).
reference.tracksNote: You can register for both programs, but each registration needs its own documents and its own $50 fee, and each is scored by its own aptitude test/PEF. If you're offered a spot in both, EJATT requires you to choose one — you cannot be enrolled in both programs at the same time. Registration for both programs happens at the same place and time (every Wednesday, 9–11am, Alsip), so a student can register for one or both on the same visit.
reference.apply: Registration is handled directly through EJATT / the IBEW-NECA Technical Institute — walk in on a Wednesday morning in Alsip (bring documents for whichever program(s) you're registering for), or email Registration@in-techonline.org / check ejatt.com for the current registration cycle first.

reference.dayInLife: Most days on an IBEW Local 134 job start on-site early, reading commercial blueprints to figure out where power needs to run before pulling conduit and wire. Early in the apprenticeship, a lot of the work is labor — drilling, fishing wire, cleanup — while journeymen handle terminations and panel work. As skills build through IN-Tech's classroom rotations (motor control, code, blueprints), the work shifts toward troubleshooting circuits, wiring panels, and eventually signing off on your own installs. Some days are quiet, precise indoor work in a data center or hospital; others mean coordinating with a full crew on a high-rise in the Loop.

steps.title: Take the Aptitude Test
steps.explanation: Applicants who submit complete documents by the deadline take the electrical trade's aptitude test, developed and validated by the American Institutes for Research (AIR) — the same organization referenced by other JATCs nationally. It's a two-part test: Part I is HS Algebra, Part II is reading comprehension. Scores range 1–9; a score of 4 or above makes an applicant eligible for an interview — though the interview pool itself may be capped at roughly 500% of anticipated openings, so a qualifying score doesn't guarantee an interview slot. For the 2027 class, the test is given in November 2026; you'll be notified of your specific date/time by email and in your TradeSchool account.

steps.explanation: Applicants interviewed from the eligible pool who are selected must then pass a physical examination and a drug test (including marijuana) before being formally indentured as an apprentice — indenture itself requires being at least 18 years old, even though the minimum age to apply is 17. For the 2027 class, interviews run January–February 2027; selection from the resulting eligibility list depends on how many job openings exist, with work beginning in spring 2027 and classes starting fall 2027.

options: Both rotate at the same speed
questions.explanation: Belt speed is the same for both pulleys. A smaller pulley has a smaller circumference, so it must complete more rotations per minute to keep up with the same belt speed.

questions.explanation: A lever balances when weight × distance matches on both sides: 15 × 3 = 45. To balance with 9 lbs: 45 ÷ 9 = 5 feet.

reference.dayInLife: A Local 597 pipefitter's day depends heavily on which of the four programs they're in. Building Trades pipefitters measure, fabricate, connect, and install piping for steam, water, air, and process systems inside commercial and industrial buildings — hospitals, steel mills, food-processing plants. HVAC and HVAC Control apprentices split time between contractor work and classroom instruction one day a week for the full five years. Gas Distributors apprentices, by contrast, work almost entirely outdoors, often inside excavations, installing and maintaining plastic and steel gas mains across residential neighborhoods and rural farmland. Early years mean a lot of physical prep work and hands-on skill-building; later years bring more independent layout and problem-solving.

questions.prompt: Three gears are meshed in a row — Gear 1 turns Gear 2, and Gear 2 turns Gear 3. If Gear 1 turns clockwise, which direction does Gear 3 turn?
questions.explanation: Each meshing reverses direction: Gear 1→Gear 2 reverses once, Gear 2→Gear 3 reverses again — two reversals cancel out, so Gear 3 turns the same direction as Gear 1.

questions.prompt: Two pulleys are turned by the same motor at the same rotational speed (RPM). Pulley A has a small diameter; Pulley B has a large diameter. Whose rope moves faster?

questions.prompt: A lever is balanced on a fulcrum. A 10-lb weight sits 4 feet from the fulcrum on one side. How far from the fulcrum must a 5-lb weight be placed on the other side to balance it?
questions.explanation: A lever balances when weight × distance is equal on both sides: 10 × 4 = 40. To balance with 5 lbs: 40 ÷ 5 = 8 feet.

questions.prompt: In a basic hydraulic system, a small-area piston pushes fluid into a much larger-area piston. Compared to the force applied at the small piston, the force produced at the large piston is:
questions.explanation: Hydraulic systems amplify force based on the ratio of piston areas — pushing fluid from a small piston into a larger one multiplies the output force, which is the whole point of hydraulic lifts and jacks.

questions.explanation: 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225. √225 = 15 feet — the same 3-4-5 ratio scaled up, a common on-the-job shortcut for squaring corners.

For Local 63 Building specifically: an ACT WorkKeys® Assessment Score Report (Applied Math, Workplace Documents, Graphic Literacy) dated within one year of applying

If applicable: military training certifications (DD-214) or existing welding certifications can strengthen an application

steps.title: Complete testing & interview
steps.explanation: For Local 63 Building applicants: submit your ACT WorkKeys® score report with your application, then pass an HPE (Human Performance Evaluation/agility test) and a physical. Applicants are ranked by score, and top scorers are given an interview before being indentured as an apprentice. (Local 1 and Local 63's Fence Erectors program may follow a different process — confirm directly.)

steps.title: Classroom + on-the-job training
steps.explanation:
Local 63: apprentices attend class ~23 hours a month, September through May, on evenings and weekends

Local 1: a school year runs 40 weeks (late August–June), evenings 5–8 or 9pm, minimum 2 evenings/week

steps.title: Journeyman Ironworker/Welder
steps.explanation: Full journeyman status with your local, portable within the national Ironworkers system.

steps.title: Take any building/construction coursework at your high school or community college
steps.explanation: Examples of courses are construction safety, shop, drafting, or basic arc welding. These count as real experience on an application, even without a job in the trade yet.

steps.title: Practice questions for the entrance exam
steps.explanation: Found on this trade's own page, right after the roadmap steps — look for the “Try Practice Questions” button. Going in familiar with the exam format strengthens an application, even before a test date is scheduled.

questions.prompt: A welder needs to bevel the edge of a steel plate at a 37.5-degree angle for a weld joint. If the bevel angle is doubled, what is the new angle?
A roll of welding wire weighs 44 pounds. How many ounces is that? (1 lb = 16 oz)
What number comes next in the series: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ___
questions.explanation: The gaps increase by 2 each time (4, 6, 8, 10…), so the next gap is 12: 30 + 12 = 42.

questions.prompt: Passage: “Ironworkers Local 63 accepts applications year-round through an online portal, with no fixed application window. Local 1, which trains a different specialty of ironwork, does not keep applications open at all times — it posts openings only when a new class is about to begin, and otherwise applications remain closed until further notice.” Which statement is best supported?
options: Both locals accept applications at any time.
One local has an ongoing application process while the other opens only periodically.
Local 1 accepts more applicants than Local 63.
questions.explanation: Local 63 is described as year-round; Local 1 is described as posting openings only periodically — that's a real, meaningful difference between the two real tracks.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most important to confirm before striking an arc during welding?
options: That proper PPE (helmet, gloves) is being worn
The price of steel that day
The color of the welding cable
questions.explanation: Arc welding produces intense UV light, heat, and sparks — proper PPE is a baseline safety check before starting, every time.

questions.prompt: A welder needs a 90° corner joint made from two mitered pieces of angle iron. If one piece is cut at 45°, what angle must the mating piece be cut at?
questions.explanation: Two equal miter cuts must add up to the 90° corner: 90 ÷ 2 = 45° each.

questions.prompt: A spool of welding wire weighs 33 pounds. How many ounces is that? (1 lb = 16 oz)
A weld bead is ⅜ inch wide, then built up an additional ¼ inch. What is the total width?
questions.explanation: ¼ = ²⁄₈. ⅜ + ²⁄₈ = ⁵⁄₈ in.

questions.prompt: A welding job estimates a 5% rework rate on 240 completed welds. How many welds are expected to need rework?
A welder completes 8 welds per hour. How many welds are completed in a 9-hour shift?
questions.explanation: 8 × 9 = 72 welds.

questions.prompt: Passage: “GTAW (TIG) welding produces a cleaner, more precise weld than some other processes, but is generally slower. FCAW (flux-cored arc welding) works faster and is often preferred for thicker material or outdoor conditions, where wind might otherwise disrupt a shielding gas.” Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: TIG welding is always faster than FCAW.
Different welding processes suit different job conditions and needs.
FCAW can never be used outdoors.
There is only one correct welding process for every job.
questions.explanation: The passage describes TIG as cleaner but slower, and FCAW as faster and better suited to thick material or wind — different processes fit different situations, not one universal answer.

questions.prompt: A welder is about to work in a confined space with limited ventilation. What is the most important safety precaution to take first?
options: Begin welding immediately to finish quickly
Ensure proper ventilation or fume extraction is in place
Skip PPE since the space is small
questions.explanation: Welding fumes build up quickly in confined spaces — confirming ventilation or fume extraction before starting is a basic safety requirement, not an optional step.

questions.prompt: Which welding process uses a continuously fed wire electrode and shielding gas, and is generally considered easier to learn than stick welding?
questions.explanation: GMAW, or MIG welding, feeds a continuous wire electrode through the gun along with a shielding gas — its more automatic wire feed makes it a common starting point for new welders.

questions.prompt: What number comes next in the series: 1, 3, 7, 13, 21, ___
questions.explanation: The gaps increase by 2 each time (2, 4, 6, 8…), so the next gap is 10: 21 + 10 = 31.

reference.description: A welder fuses metal parts together using heat, pressure, or both — work that shows up inside almost every other trade rather than standing alone as its own single apprenticeship. In the Chicago area, welding is taught through the Ironworkers, split across two different locals depending on the kind of work: architectural/ornamental metalwork (railings, stairs, curtain walls, fencing) through Local 63 in Broadview, and structural/bridge/reinforcing ironwork through Local 1 in Forest Park.
reference.blurb: Fuses metal parts together using heat — taught here through two Ironworkers locals.

tracks.name: Architectural & Ornamental / Building (Local 63)
tracks.short: Welds railings, stairs, curtain walls, and architectural metal and glass systems.
tracks.covers: Window walls, glass, and metal rails, curtain walls, storefronts, glass & metal doors, stairs, scaffolds, fire escapes, canopies, and skylights — using GTAW, FCAW, and SMAW welding processes plus oxy-acetylene cutting. Minimum 200 classroom hours/year plus 1,400 paid OJT hours/year. Trains in Broadview, IL.

tracks.name: Fence Erectors (Local 63)
tracks.short: Installs and repairs chain-link fencing and related metal framework.
tracks.covers: A genuinely separate apprenticeship program at the same Local 63, covering chain-link fence setup, relocation, repair, and sheet-metal fence framework, guard rails, and erosion/snow fencing. Minimum 160 classroom hours/year plus 1,400 paid OJT hours/year — fewer classroom hours than the Building program. Same Broadview, IL training center.

tracks.name: Structural, Bridge & Reinforcing (Local 1)
tracks.short: Erects structural steel and places reinforcing steel on buildings and bridges.
tracks.covers: Structural steel erection, reinforcing steel placement, bridgework, rigging, post-tensioning, precast concrete structures, and crane assembly/disassembly. Trains in Forest Park, IL. Applications are not always open — Local 1 posts “applications closed until further notice” between cycles.

reference.tracksIntro: Both are real, separate Ironworkers locals with separate applications — a student applies to one or the other, based on the kind of ironwork/welding that interests them.
reference.tracksNote: Local 63 alone runs two genuinely separate programs (Building and Fence Erectors), each with its own classroom-hour requirement; Local 1 is a fully separate local with its own 3-year program. Confirm which program a student means before assuming “Local 63” means just one thing.
wageRows: Confirmed pattern: roughly 10% pay increases based on hours worked, until journey level — exact starting percentage not published
Journeyman, structural iron & steel workers (BLS, May 2024)
Not published in sources found — contact the local directly
reference.toolsNote: Torch and welding-specific tools aren't listed here — those come once cutting or welding work is a regular part of the job, not on day one.
reference.apply: Apply directly with whichever local matches the ironwork/welding track a student wants — Local 63 accepts applications year-round for both its Building and Fence programs (apprenticetraining@amts63.com), or check Local 1's site directly for the next open application window.
reference.practiceNote: No free published practice material was found for either local's selection process.
reference.dayInLife: An ironworker/welder's day depends on the track. Architectural/ornamental welders (Local 63) often work on-site fitting and welding railings, stairs, and curtain-wall systems into buildings — precise, detail-oriented work, sometimes at height. Structural ironworkers (Local 1) more often work erecting structural steel, placing reinforcing steel, and doing bridgework — outdoors, at height, on active construction sites, with rigging and crane work a regular part of the job.
